Proposition 2 : Larger state rainy day fund
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 2 would change the State Constitution so the state keeps saving in its main rainy day fund until the fund equals 20% of General Fund taxes, up from 10% today, and saves more in years when revenue from investment gains is very high. It would also extend required extra debt payments from 2030 to 2040 and stop counting rainy day fund deposits toward the state spending limit until the money is taken out.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 2 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 2
Rainy day fund cap 10% of General Fund taxes today; 20% if Prop 2 passes
Rainy day fund balance $15.1 billion projected at the end of 2026-27 (Assembly Budget Committee)
Vote needed Simple majority
Legislature's vote Assembly 59-8, Senate 29-2 (June 25, 2026)
Money raised For: $383,715.57 from July 1 to Nov. 1, 2026, by one committee controlled by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel. Against: no committee
Outside spending Against: $40,500 by Reform California (shared with other props). For: about $70,000, mostly shared with other props
Latest public poll PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 61% yes, 38% no (likely voters)
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures are from state campaign filings in the Secretary of State's Cal-Access database.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , The details , How it got on the ballot , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 2 mean?
Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
What does a no vote on Proposition 2 mean?
Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
What would Proposition 2 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says state budget reserves would be higher, which would make it somewhat easier to balance the budget when revenue falls. The state might also make more debt payments than it would otherwise. The analysis gives no dollar figure.
What it means for the City of LA
Proposition 2 changes only state accounts. It does not change the City of Los Angeles's own reserve rules or spending limit, and the Legislative Analyst does not estimate any local effect. Its effect on the City would come through the state budget, which pays for programs the City relies on, such as state homelessness grants. A larger state reserve is meant to make state cuts less likely in a downturn, but the measure does not guarantee any program's funding.
The details
Official title Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Legislative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by the Legislature (ACA 20, Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026)
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide. Under the State Constitution (Article XVIII, Section 4), an amendment takes effect if "approved by a majority of votes cast thereon."
The question on your ballot
Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. Fiscal Impact: State budget reserves would be higher. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel Opponents: None submitted
This is not the Proposition 2 on the November 5, 2024 ballot, the bond for public school and college facilities, which passed with 58.7% of the vote (Secretary of State, November 2024 Statement of Vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-general/sov/59-state-ballot-measures.pdf)).
What would change
Today If Proposition 2 passes
Rainy day fund cap Deposits stop once the fund reaches 10% of General Fund taxes; money that would have gone in must go to infrastructure (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)) Deposits continue until the fund reaches 20% (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm))
Yearly set-aside 1.5% of General Fund tax revenue, half to the rainy day fund and half to debt payments, plus extra when capital gains revenue tops 8% of General Fund taxes (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)) The 1.5% stays. Capital gains revenue between 8% and 10% of General Fund taxes still counts as extra; above 10%, 1.5 times the amount counts (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/); text, Sec. 20 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1))
Extra debt payments Required through 2030, and only for state pension and retiree health debts (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)) Required through 2040. Can also go to money owed to schools and community colleges, loans from other state funds, and federal unemployment insurance loans (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm))
State spending limit (Gann limit) Money put into the rainy day fund counts toward the limit when deposited (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)) Starting in 2027-28, deposits do not count; withdrawals count when taken out. The same applies to the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account, up to 10% of General Fund taxes a year (text, Sec. 20(i)-(j) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Declaring a budget emergency The Governor must issue a proclamation before deposits can be cut or money withdrawn (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)) The Governor’s May budget revision counts as the proclamation if it proposes cutting deposits or withdrawing money and emergency conditions exist (text, Sec. 22(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4))
School funding guarantee (Prop. 98) Unchanged Unchanged. The text says nothing in it “is intended to change the calculation or funding of the minimum guarantee” (text, First (b)(8) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1))
What stays the same: the state can still cut deposits or withdraw money in a budget emergency, with the same definition of emergency. No more than half the fund can be withdrawn in the first year of an emergency. Required debt payments still cannot be suspended (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
No direct change for the City. Proposition 2 amends only Sections 20 and 22 of Article XVI of the State Constitution, which govern state reserves (ACA 20 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)). The Legislative Analyst’s analysis covers only the state budget (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)).
The City’s own reserves follow City policy. The City’s Reserve Fund must equal 5% of General Fund revenue, and the City’s goal is 10% across its Reserve Fund, Budget Stabilization Fund and unappropriated balance (City 2026-27 Proposed Budget, General Fund Reserves Policy (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf#page=24)). Proposition 2 does not change these.
Indirect effect through the state budget. The City budgets state money for some programs, such as the state’s Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention (HHAP) grants (City 2026-27 Proposed Budget (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf)). The Analyst says higher reserves “would make balancing the budget somewhat easier when revenues decline” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)). The measure does not set aside money for any local program. The Budget Center says money set aside in boom years would not be available then for needs such as “support for local governments to address homelessness” (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)).
The Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce is one of the signers of the argument in favor (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/arguments-rebuttals.htm)). We found no City Council position on Proposition 2 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
ACA 20 needed a two-thirds vote of each house (ACA 20 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)). It was filed with the Secretary of State without a Governor’s signature (ACA 20 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)).
June 22, 2026: ACA 20 was introduced. Its lead authors are Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Valencia and Senators Hurtado and John Laird. The Assembly voted 51-16 to suspend two of its rules the same day (ACA 20 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20); ACA 20 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)).
June 25, 2026: The Assembly tabled amendments offered by Assemblymember David Tangipa, 55-18, then adopted ACA 20, 59-8. The Senate withdrew it from committee and adopted it the same day, 29-2. It was filed as Resolution Chapter 130 (ACA 20 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20); ACA 20 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)). The Assembly no votes were DeMaio, Dixon, Ellis, Hadwick, Macedo, Patterson, Sanchez and Tangipa. The Senate no votes were Choi and Grove (ACA 20 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)).
The Governor’s office listed the amendment as part of the 2026-27 budget agreement announced June 26 (Governor’s office (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/06/26/finalbudget/)). The Assembly Budget Committee’s floor report says the rainy day fund changes were “completed in conjunction with legislative approval of ACA 20” (Assembly floor report, p. 6 (https://abgt.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-06/floor-report-of-the-2026-27-budget-june-27-2026_5.pdf#page=6)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. The State Constitution says a proposed amendment “shall be submitted to the electors and, if approved by a majority of votes cast thereon, takes effect” (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)).
Related past measures.
Proposition 58 (2004) created the rainy day fund, the Budget Stabilization Account (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)).
Proposition 2 (November 2014) set the current deposit, debt payment and 10% cap rules (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)). It passed with 69.1% statewide and 69.8% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2014 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2014-general/pdf/88-ballot-measures.pdf)).
Proposition 4 (1979) created the state spending limit, known as the Gann limit (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument in favor, signed by Darrell Roberts of California Professional Firefighters, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel and Maria S. Salinas of the Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
The state budget swung “from a $100 billion surplus to a $50 billion deficit in just a few years.”
It doubles the reserve requirement “so California has a real cushion.”
It makes the state bank more of a revenue spike “instead of committing it to new ongoing spending.”
The Legislative Analyst “has recommended that the state should be saving significantly more than current rules require.”
Their rebuttal, signed by Linda Darling-Hammond of the State Board of Education, Carmela Coyle of the California Hospital Association and Francisco J. Silva of the California Primary Care Association, calls the taxpayer rebate “a 50-year-old accounting gimmick that rewards spending instead of saving” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument against, signed by Assemblymember David Tangipa, Sen. Steven Choi and Carl DeMaio of Reform California (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
It lets politicians “gut the voter-imposed spending limit” and creates a “SLUSH FUND.”
It “cancels your tax rebate,” which the Constitution requires when revenue exceeds the spending limit.
The state budget “has grown by 76% since 2018.”
“Within 24 hours” of putting it on the ballot, the same politicians “voted to suspend more than $5 billion in required deposits.”
Outside the guide.
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association recommends a no vote. Its guide says the measure’s reserve changes make sense “from the perspective of addressing revenue volatility” but calls it “little more than a Band-Aid on a severed limb” because it does not undo earlier changes to the Gann limit (HJTA 2026 voting guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/)).
Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón said the budget deal addresses “our short and long-term financial future by building up our rainy day fund” (Governor’s office (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/06/26/finalbudget/)).
Checking the main factual claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What the records show
The Legislative Analyst recommended saving more Yes campaign In February 2026 the Analyst recommended raising the cap to 50% by 2055, starting with 20% “immediately after the next statewide election.” It estimated current rules would cover about 30% of future funding shortfalls (LAO handout, Feb. 18, 2026, p. 7 (https://sbud.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2026-02/lao-handout-2.18-hearing.pdf#page=7)).
Prop 2 cancels taxpayer rebates No campaign If revenue exceeds the limit two years in a row, the excess is split between taxpayers and schools (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)). Prop 2 takes rainy day fund deposits, and holding account deposits up to 10% of General Fund taxes, out of the limit until withdrawn (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)). That lowers counted spending in deposit years, which makes an excess less likely then. The Analyst does not estimate the effect on rebates (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)).
Lawmakers suspended more than $5 billion in deposits within 24 hours No campaign The Assembly floor report says 2025-26 “true up” deposits to the rainy day fund “remain suspended” under the 2026-27 budget (Assembly floor report, p. 10 (https://abgt.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-06/floor-report-of-the-2026-27-budget-june-27-2026_5.pdf#page=10)). The report does not give the amount. The same package raises reserves to an estimated $28.8 billion, including $15.1 billion in the rainy day fund (same page (https://abgt.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-06/floor-report-of-the-2026-27-budget-june-27-2026_5.pdf#page=10)).
Prop 2 makes the budget more volatile No campaign The Analyst says more reserves “would make balancing the budget somewhat easier when revenues decline” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)).
Education funding is protected Yes campaign The text says it does not change the Prop. 98 guarantee (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1)). The rebuttal to the argument in favor says Prop 2 dedicates no new dollars to schools, health care or public safety (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/arguments-rebuttals.htm)). Both are consistent with the text.
We did not check the “$100 billion surplus to $50 billion deficit” or “76% since 2018” figures against official budget records.
Who supports and opposes it
Supporters
On the ballot label: California Professional Firefighters, Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce, Gov. Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra and Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (ballot label (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/)).
The campaign’s coalition list adds Speaker Robert Rivas, Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón, SEIU California, the California Hospital Association, California Primary Care Association, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, State Board of Education President Linda Darling-Hammond, 21st Century Alliance and California Environmental Voters (Yes on Prop 2 (https://yesonprop2.com/)).
California Democratic Party (CDP positions, Aug. 2, 2026 (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf)).
League of Women Voters of California (LWVC recommendations (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/)).
California State PTA, which voted to support on Aug. 8, 2026 (CAPTA (https://capta.org/advocacy/state-ballot-measures/)).

Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (HJTA 2026 voting guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/)).
The legislators who voted no, listed above (ACA 20 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)).
Editorial boards and others. The Daily News editorial board recommends no: “Vote no on Prop. 2 and elect more prudent state lawmakers” (Daily News, Oct. 7, 2026 (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/10/07/endorsement-no-on-prop-2-california-needs-fiscal-discipline-not-accounting-tricks/)). The Mercury News and East Bay Times editorial boards list a yes vote in their endorsements roundup (Mercury News, Oct. 13, 2026 (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/13/bay-area-news-group-california-election-endorsements-november-2026/)). The San Diego Union-Tribune editorial board recommends no: “No on Proposition 2” (San Diego Union-Tribune, Oct. 2, 2026 (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/02/endorsements-props-2-37-wouldnt-yield-saner-state-budgets-more-housing/)). The San Francisco Chronicle editorial board recommends yes: “Voters should pass Prop 2 and hold lawmakers accountable to their promise to be more responsible stewards of taxpayer money” (SF Chronicle, Oct. 15, 2026 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-2-money-california-22468892.php)). We found no LA Times editorial board position as of Sept. 30, 2026, and no published position from the California Republican Party. The California Budget & Policy Center analyzed the measure without taking a position (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)).
Money for and against
For Proposition 2 Against Proposition 2
Committees One: Yes on Proposition 2, a Ballot Measure Committee Controlled by Jesse Gabriel (ID 1485332) None registered
Raised, July 1 to Sept. 19, 2026 $65,038.90 $0
Raised, Sept. 20 to Oct. 17 $308,877.29 $0
Raised, Oct. 18 to Nov. 1 (late reports) $9,799.38 $0
Spent, July 1 to Oct. 17 $299,876.45, of which $125,243 was unpaid bills $0
Cash on hand, Oct. 17 $257,832.74 $0
Independent spending, through Oct. 25 $70,166.82 (mostly shared with other props) $43,205.53 (mostly shared with other props)
Source: the committee’s campaign statements (July 1-Sept. 19 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3199850&amendid=0); Sept. 20-Oct. 17 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3216152&amendid=0); 2025 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3115256&amendid=0)) and late contribution reports filed through Nov. 1 (including the Oct. 21 report (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3214499&amendid=0)), from the Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip) of Nov. 2, analyzed by CityHallPass. The Secretary of State’s contribution totals page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-2-aca-20-gabriel-save-californias-future-act-res-ch-130-2026) still listed no committees, as of its Aug. 2 update, when checked on Sept. 30.
The committee was called “United for Justice, A Ballot Measure Committee Controlled by Jesse Gabriel” until June 30, 2026, and took its Proposition 2 name with the July-September statement. Its Sept. 20-Oct. 17 statement uses the name “Californians for a Responsible Budget, Yes on Proposition 2, a Ballot Measure Committee Controlled by Jesse Gabriel” (Sept. 20-Oct. 17 statement (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3216152&amendid=0)). Before July it raised $67,075.09, mostly a $48,950 transfer from another Gabriel committee, Californians for Justice, in December 2025 (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip); 2025 statement (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3115256&amendid=0)).
Who is giving
Method: every itemized contribution to committee 1485332 from Jan. 1, 2025 through Oct. 17, 2026, plus late reports filed through Nov. 1, from the Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip), analyzed by CityHallPass.
Donor Amount Share of $450,790.66
Google LLC and affiliated entities (Oct. 5, 2026) $150,000 33.3%
California Democratic Party (in-kind literature, postage, staff and voter data, Sept. 10 to Oct. 26, 2026) $58,715.57 13.0%
SEIU California State Council Small Contributor Committee (Sept. 18, 2026) $50,000 11.1%
21st Century Alliance (Sept. 21, 2026) $50,000 11.1%
SEIU Local 2015 Issues Committee (Oct. 9, 2026) $50,000 11.1%
Californians for Justice, a Ballot Measure Committee Controlled by Jesse Gabriel (Dec. 2025 and Jan. 2026) $49,000 10.9%
Centene and its affiliate Health Net (in-kind, fundraiser, Jan. 2026) $18,075.09 4.0%
California Professional Firefighters Ballot Issues Committee (Oct. 8, 2026) $15,000 3.3%
One individual (Sept. 11, 2026) $10,000 2.2%
Source: Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip) and the committee’s July-Sept. 19 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3199850&amendid=0) and Sept. 20-Oct. 17 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3216152&amendid=0) statements, analyzed by CityHallPass.
All nine donors have California addresses. Since the committee took its Proposition 2 name, the money has come from Google, two SEIU committees, a business-backed group (21st Century Alliance), the firefighters’ union committee, the Democratic Party and one individual. The committee did not reach the $1 million level that triggers an FPPC top-10 list (FPPC top-10 list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/)).
How the money was spent. The committee reported $299,876.45 in spending for July 1 to Oct. 17. Of that, $125,717.26 was paid out, $48,916.19 was in-kind help counted as spending, and $125,243 was bills not yet paid. It reported $143,567.85 in unpaid bills on Oct. 17. Payments included $65,000 to David Binder Research for polling, $20,000 each to Click Strategies and Polaris Campaigns for consulting, $7,500 to LAFC StadiumCo for fundraising events and $7,500 to the COPS Voter Guide (July-Sept. statement (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3199850&amendid=0); Sept. 20-Oct. 17 statement (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3216152&amendid=0)). The statement data we used do not name the vendors owed the unpaid bills.
Outside spending
Independent expenditures reported through Oct. 25, 2026 (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip) of Oct. 26):
Against: Reform California with Carl DeMaio (ID 1268914) reported $40,500 for slate mailers, door hangers and campaign management on July 1, Aug. 27 and Oct. 1. The same payments are listed against several other propositions, so the Proposition 2 share cannot be separated. The Republican Party of San Diego County reported $2,705.53 for member literature on Oct. 5.
For: 10 committees reported $70,166.82. Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California VOTES PAC reported $34,293.58 for digital ads and its voter guide (Oct. 13 to 15) and GrowSF $14,511.76 for digital ads. The other eight, including SPUR, Million Voter Project Action Fund, Youth Power PAC, two United Domestic Workers committees and the California Democratic Party, reported $21,361.48 together. Most of these items are shared with other propositions.
Independent analysis
Legislative Analyst. Besides the official analysis (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)), the Analyst says revenue declines over a bad recession “can equal 50 percent or more of annual General Fund revenues.” In a February presentation to the Senate Budget Committee, its simulations found current rules would cover about 30% of funding shortfalls over 50 years; raising the cap to 50% by 2055 with stronger deposit rules would cover about 75% (LAO handout, pp. 6-7 (https://sbud.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2026-02/lao-handout-2.18-hearing.pdf#page=7)). The handout does not model Proposition 2 as written.
Budget Center. The California Budget & Policy Center says that if Prop 2’s capital gains rules had applied from 2010-11 to 2023-24, the state would have set aside more in six of those 14 years, less than 1% to 2% of General Fund revenue each time. It says the change could take hundreds of millions of dollars, or more than $1 billion, off the table in some years. It also says a higher cap means less “spillover” money for infrastructure, and that using debt payments on federal unemployment insurance loans would shift a cost from businesses to the state (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)).
Current reserves. The 2026-27 budget projects $28.8 billion in reserves: $15.1 billion in the rainy day fund, $9.2 billion in the school reserve and $4.5 billion in the operating reserve, plus $6.4 billion in the temporary holding account (Assembly floor report, p. 10 (https://abgt.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-06/floor-report-of-the-2026-27-budget-june-27-2026_5.pdf#page=10)).
Interaction with other measures on this ballot
The Legislative Analyst’s analysis names no conflict between Proposition 2 and other measures on this ballot (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)).
Proposition 41 also deals with the state spending limit, in a different way: it would stop new state taxes from being excluded from the limit (LAO analysis of Prop 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/analysis.htm)). Proposition 2 concerns reserve deposits, not taxes. See our Proposition 41 page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-41).
Proposition 3 would keep higher income tax rates on high earners after 2031 (Prop 3 analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). Rainy day fund deposits are set as shares of General Fund revenue, so more revenue means larger required deposits under either current rules or Proposition 2 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)). See our Proposition 3 page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-03).
If it passes
When it takes effect. A constitutional amendment takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)). The spending limit changes apply starting in the 2027-28 fiscal year (text, Sec. 20(i) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)).
Budget emergencies. The Governor could use the May budget revision as the emergency proclamation (text, Sec. 22(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4)).
Debt payments. The Assembly Budget Committee says the new debt payment rules would give the state another way to pay an estimated $3.9 billion owed to schools and community colleges for 2025-26 (Assembly floor report, p. 6 (https://abgt.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-06/floor-report-of-the-2026-27-budget-june-27-2026_5.pdf#page=6)).
Legal challenges. We found no reported legal challenge as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Key moments
We found no debate focused on Proposition 2 in news coverage as of Sept. 30, 2026.
LAO reserve recommendations (Feb. 18, 2026). The Analyst recommended raising the rainy day fund cap to 50% by 2055 (LAO handout (https://sbud.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2026-02/lao-handout-2.18-hearing.pdf)).
Budget deal and three-day passage (June 22-25, 2026). ACA 20 was introduced June 22 and adopted by both houses June 25, alongside the 2026-27 budget (ACA 20 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20); Governor’s office (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/06/26/finalbudget/)).
Committee renamed (July 2026). Gabriel’s ballot committee took the Yes on Proposition 2 name (July-Sept. statement (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3199850&amendid=0)).
Polls

October: PPIC likely voter tables (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf). Source: PPIC, September 2026, pp. 6-7, 22 and 29 (https://www.ppic.org/pdf/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026.pdf#page=6). Respondents read the ballot title and label. Support was 82% among Democrats, 22% among Republicans and 60% among independents. One percent of likely voters named Proposition 2 as the measure they were most interested in. We found no other public poll on Proposition 2.

Independent analysis
Legislative Analyst. Besides the official analysis (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)), the Analyst says revenue declines over a bad recession “can equal 50 percent or more of annual General Fund revenues.” In a February presentation to the Senate Budget Committee, its simulations found current rules would cover about 30% of funding shortfalls over 50 years; raising the cap to 50% by 2055 with stronger deposit rules would cover about 75% (LAO handout, pp. 6-7 (https://sbud.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2026-02/lao-handout-2.18-hearing.pdf#page=7)). The handout does not model Proposition 2 as written.
Budget Center. The California Budget & Policy Center says that if Prop 2’s capital gains rules had applied from 2010-11 to 2023-24, the state would have set aside more in six of those 14 years, less than 1% to 2% of General Fund revenue each time. It says the change could take hundreds of millions of dollars, or more than $1 billion, off the table in some years. It also says a higher cap means less “spillover” money for infrastructure, and that using debt payments on federal unemployment insurance loans would shift a cost from businesses to the state (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)).
Current reserves. The 2026-27 budget projects $28.8 billion in reserves: $15.1 billion in the rainy day fund, $9.2 billion in the school reserve and $4.5 billion in the operating reserve, plus $6.4 billion in the temporary holding account (Assembly floor report, p. 10 (https://abgt.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-06/floor-report-of-the-2026-27-budget-june-27-2026_5.pdf#page=10)).
Interaction with other measures on this ballot
The Legislative Analyst’s analysis names no conflict between Proposition 2 and other measures on this ballot (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)).
Proposition 41 also deals with the state spending limit, in a different way: it would stop new state taxes from being excluded from the limit (LAO analysis of Prop 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/analysis.htm)). Proposition 2 concerns reserve deposits, not taxes. See our Proposition 41 page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-41).
Proposition 3 would keep higher income tax rates on high earners after 2031 (Prop 3 analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). Rainy day fund deposits are set as shares of General Fund revenue, so more revenue means larger required deposits under either current rules or Proposition 2 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)). See our Proposition 3 page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-03).
If it passes
When it takes effect. A constitutional amendment takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)). The spending limit changes apply starting in the 2027-28 fiscal year (text, Sec. 20(i) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)).
Budget emergencies. The Governor could use the May budget revision as the emergency proclamation (text, Sec. 22(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4)).
Debt payments. The Assembly Budget Committee says the new debt payment rules would give the state another way to pay an estimated $3.9 billion owed to schools and community colleges for 2025-26 (Assembly floor report, p. 6 (https://abgt.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-06/floor-report-of-the-2026-27-budget-june-27-2026_5.pdf#page=6)).
Legal challenges. We found no reported legal challenge as of Sept. 30, 2026.

Independent analysis
Legislative Analyst. Besides the official analysis (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)), the Analyst says revenue declines over a bad recession “can equal 50 percent or more of annual General Fund revenues.” In a February presentation to the Senate Budget Committee, its simulations found current rules would cover about 30% of funding shortfalls over 50 years; raising the cap to 50% by 2055 with stronger deposit rules would cover about 75% (LAO handout, pp. 6-7 (https://sbud.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2026-02/lao-handout-2.18-hearing.pdf#page=7)). The handout does not model Proposition 2 as written.
Budget Center. The California Budget & Policy Center says that if Prop 2’s capital gains rules had applied from 2010-11 to 2023-24, the state would have set aside more in six of those 14 years, less than 1% to 2% of General Fund revenue each time. It says the change could take hundreds of millions of dollars, or more than $1 billion, off the table in some years. It also says a higher cap means less “spillover” money for infrastructure, and that using debt payments on federal unemployment insurance loans would shift a cost from businesses to the state (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)).
Current reserves. The 2026-27 budget projects $28.8 billion in reserves: $15.1 billion in the rainy day fund, $9.2 billion in the school reserve and $4.5 billion in the operating reserve, plus $6.4 billion in the temporary holding account (Assembly floor report, p. 10 (https://abgt.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-06/floor-report-of-the-2026-27-budget-june-27-2026_5.pdf#page=10)).
Interaction with other measures on this ballot
The Legislative Analyst’s analysis names no conflict between Proposition 2 and other measures on this ballot (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)).
Proposition 41 also deals with the state spending limit, in a different way: it would stop new state taxes from being excluded from the limit (LAO analysis of Prop 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/analysis.htm)). Proposition 2 concerns reserve deposits, not taxes. See our Proposition 41 page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-41).
Proposition 3 would keep higher income tax rates on high earners after 2031 (Prop 3 analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). Rainy day fund deposits are set as shares of General Fund revenue, so more revenue means larger required deposits under either current rules or Proposition 2 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)). See our Proposition 3 page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-03).
If it passes
When it takes effect. A constitutional amendment takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)). The spending limit changes apply starting in the 2027-28 fiscal year (text, Sec. 20(i) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)).
Budget emergencies. The Governor could use the May budget revision as the emergency proclamation (text, Sec. 22(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4)).
Debt payments. The Assembly Budget Committee says the new debt payment rules would give the state another way to pay an estimated $3.9 billion owed to schools and community colleges for 2025-26 (Assembly floor report, p. 6 (https://abgt.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-06/floor-report-of-the-2026-27-budget-june-27-2026_5.pdf#page=6)).
Legal challenges. We found no reported legal challenge as of Sept. 30, 2026.

### Proposition 2
#### SAVE FOR CALIFORNIA’S FUTURE ACT
Proposition 2 will allow California to save more money during strong economic years so it can protect schools and other essential services when revenues fall.
California’s budget can change dramatically from one year to the next.
The state relies heavily on personal income taxes, including taxes on capital gains.
Capital gains are profits people earn when they sell stocks, businesses, real estate, or other investments.
These taxes bring in much more money when financial markets are doing well, but that revenue can disappear quickly during an economic downturn.
Prop 2 would help California prepare for those swings.
It would allow the state to build a larger rainy-day fund and require it to save more when capital gains revenues are unusually high.
That would give California a stronger financial cushion during recessions, natural disasters, public health emergencies, and other difficult periods.
Saving more during good years can help prevent deep cuts to public services during bad years.

For: 10 committees reported $70,166.82. Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California VOTES PAC reported $34,293.58 for digital ads and its voter guide (Oct. 13 to 15) and GrowSF $14,511.76 for digital ads. The other eight, including SPUR, Million Voter Project Action Fund, Youth Power PAC, two United Domestic Workers committees and the California Democratic Party, reported $21,361.48 together. Most of these items are shared with other propositions.
Independent analysis
Legislative Analyst. Besides the official analysis (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)), the Analyst says revenue declines over a bad recession “can equal 50 percent or more of annual General Fund revenues.” In a February presentation to the Senate Budget Committee, its simulations found current rules would cover about 30% of funding shortfalls over 50 years; raising the cap to 50% by 2055 with stronger deposit rules would cover about 75% (LAO handout, pp. 6-7 (https://sbud.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2026-02/lao-handout-2.18-hearing.pdf#page=7)). The handout does not model Proposition 2 as written.
Budget Center. The California Budget & Policy Center says that if Prop 2’s capital gains rules had applied from 2010-11 to 2023-24, the state would have set aside more in six of those 14 years, less than 1% to 2% of General Fund revenue each time. It says the change could take hundreds of millions of dollars, or more than $1 billion, off the table in some years. It also says a higher cap means less “spillover” money for infrastructure, and that using debt payments on federal unemployment insurance loans would shift a cost from businesses to the state (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-proposition-2-how-californias-rainy-day-fund-would-be-updated/)).
Current reserves. The 2026-27 budget projects $28.8 billion in reserves: $15.1 billion in the rainy day fund, $9.2 billion in the school reserve and $4.5 billion in the operating reserve, plus $6.4 billion in the temporary holding account (Assembly floor report, p. 10 (https://abgt.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-06/floor-report-of-the-2026-27-budget-june-27-2026_5.pdf#page=10)).
Interaction with other measures on this ballot
The Legislative Analyst’s analysis names no conflict between Proposition 2 and other measures on this ballot (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)).
Proposition 41 also deals with the state spending limit, in a different way: it would stop new state taxes from being excluded from the limit (LAO analysis of Prop 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/analysis.htm)). Proposition 2 concerns reserve deposits, not taxes. See our Proposition 41 page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-41).
Proposition 3 would keep higher income tax rates on high earners after 2031 (Prop 3 analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). Rainy day fund deposits are set as shares of General Fund revenue, so more revenue means larger required deposits under either current rules or Proposition 2 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/analysis.htm)). See our Proposition 3 page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-03).
If it passes
When it takes effect. A constitutional amendment takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)). The spending limit changes apply starting in the 2027-28 fiscal year (text, Sec. 20(i) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)).
Budget emergencies. The Governor could use the May budget revision as the emergency proclamation (text, Sec. 22(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4)).
Debt payments. The Assembly Budget Committee says the new debt payment rules would give the state another way to pay an estimated $3.9 billion owed to schools and community colleges for 2025-26 (Assembly floor report, p. 6 (https://abgt.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-06/floor-report-of-the-2026-27-budget-june-27-2026_5.pdf#page=6)).
Legal challenges. We found no reported legal challenge as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Key moments
We found no debate focused on Proposition 2 in news coverage as of Sept. 30, 2026.
LAO reserve recommendations (Feb. 18, 2026). The Analyst recommended raising the rainy day fund cap to 50% by 2055 (LAO handout (https://sbud.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2026-02/lao-handout-2.18-hearing.pdf)).
Budget deal and three-day passage (June 22-25, 2026). ACA 20 was introduced June 22 and adopted by both houses June 25, alongside the 2026-27 budget (ACA 20 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20); Governor’s office (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/06/26/finalbudget/)).
Committee renamed (July 2026). Gabriel’s ballot committee took the Yes on Proposition 2 name (July-Sept. statement (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3199850&amendid=0)).

Advocates of Proposition 2 say they want to make it easier for state lawmakers to beef up the "rainy day" fund to help pay for long-term debt such as pension obligations. But the measure would actually make it easier to raid the fund to use for short-term, non-emergency spending. Above, lawmakers are shown at the state Capitol in June. (AP)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: October 2, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
State lawmakers — the same ones who have been approving spending plans for years that the Legislative Analyst’s Office says have billions of dollars in structural deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5091) despite the California Constitution’s requirement that budgets must be balanced — want you to believe they’re actually conscientious fiscal stewards.
That’s why in 2014, they won approval of a ballot measure that was sold to voters with the claim that it would force the Legislature to set aside 1.5% of general fund revenue to beef up the state’s Budget Stabilization Account — a “rainy day” fund that could be used to pay for specific state debts, starting with unfunded pension and retirement health care obligations.
It would also divert even more money to the fund when capital-gains revenue was surging, a common event in the Golden State due to all the wealthy individuals in Silicon Valley with stock options they can cash in when times are good.
But there was a mammoth loophole: Required contributions to the fund could be reduced or suspended after the governor and a majority of the Legislature declared a “budget emergency.”
That’s exactly what has happened over and over again. “Emergencies” were declared the last three completed fiscal years even though revenue was surging.
Now state lawmakers are back with another sham. Placed directly on the ballot by the Legislature, Proposition 2 would amend the Budget Stabilization Account by lifting the cap on how much could be contributed to it — something voters are being told would strengthen the account.
But that is built on the myth that lawmakers want to contribute more. The measure’s fine print (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/26/proposition-2-isnt-about-saving-money-its-another-sacramento-shell-game/) shows its real goal: to make it even easier for the state to avoid paying down long-term unfunded obligations by allowing lawmakers to use new rainy day funds to repay recent “budget borrowing.”
No on Proposition 2. It’s another fake reform meant to make Californians think state lawmakers are actually serious about their responsibilities.
The U-T also opposes Proposition 37 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_37,_Second_Mortgage_Homebuyer_Program_and_Revenue_Bond_Initiative_(2026)), which is less cynical than Proposition 2 but is equally unlikely to live up to the promises made about it.
The measure authorizes the state to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a middle-class down payment assistance program for purchasing newly constructed homes. Backers say it is structured in a way that ensures private bond investors, not state taxpayers, are on the hook for paying back the borrowing.
Its key provision: Eligible buyers would have to be able to make a 3% cash down payment on a home, but they could secure a fixed-rate second mortgage covering up to 17% of the purchase price. This in theory eliminates the traditional expectation of a 20% down payment.
What it doesn’t do in the slightest is to address the biggest reason California has a massive housing crisis: shelter’s extreme cost. Including condos, the median home price in the state is $775,000 (https://www.noradarealestate.com/blog/california-housing-market/). Median household income is about $99,000, according to a recent Census Bureau report (https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/CA/BZA210223). Whether a home purchase involves borrowing 80% or 97% of the sale price, the great majority of families are not going to be able to pay the resulting mortgage or mortgages.
Proposition 37 advocates somehow think that allowing qualified state residents to borrow more is a magic solution to the affordability crisis. But a Zillow calculator shows that with the interest rates available in recent months, a household income of at least $265,000 per year is generally necessary to buy a $775,000 home with a 3% down payment in California. Proposition 37 doesn’t change this daunting picture at all.
There are practical ways that the state could bring down the cost of housing. Leaders could ignore turf-protecting construction trade unions and incentivize use of the sturdy, durable prefabricated homes that now have big market shares in Japan and Great Britain. They could ignore revenue-protecting trial lawyers and fix flawed state rules that incentivize lawsuits against condo builders.

Why Are California’s Revenues Volatile?
 Revenues Are Volatile. From year to year, revenues can grow very

 Reasons for Volatility. The personal income tax (PIT) makes up
most of the General Fund revenues. Taxable personal income is more
volatile than the overall economy, primarily because: (1) incomes of
high-income taxpayers are more sensitive to changes in the economy
and asset markets and (2) the state’s progressive rate structure
concentrates taxes on these volatile incomes.
 Volatility Presents Two Related but Separate Issues. Reserves,
ideally separate ones, can address two distinct challenges:
(1) forecast error, and (2) downside risk.

Limitations of the Current Reserve Policy
 A reserve policy “performs well” if it meets the central goal of
reserves—that is, it allows the state to save enough so that the state
can pay for spending on its core services when revenues drop.
 Our analysis uses simulation-based tools—similar to those used
in insurance markets and the state’s pension system—that use
information about the past to forecast many different variations of
the future. These are reported across 50 years and thousands of
simulations.

L E G I S L A T I V E A N A LY S T ’ S O F F I C E 1
Why Are California’s Revenues Volatile?
 Revenues Are Volatile. From year to year, revenues can grow very
quickly or contract quickly.
 Reasons for Volatility. The personal income tax (PIT) makes up
most of the General Fund revenues. Taxable personal income is more
volatile than the overall economy, primarily because: (1) incomes of
high-income taxpayers are more sensitive to changes in the economy
and asset markets and (2) the state’s progressive rate structure
concentrates taxes on these volatile incomes.
 Volatility Presents Two Related but Separate Issues. Reserves,
ideally separate ones, can address two distinct challenges:
(1) forecast error, and (2) downside risk.

Advocates of Proposition 2 say they want to make it easier for state lawmakers to beef up the "rainy day" fund to help pay for long-term debt such as pension obligations. But the measure would actually make it easier to raid the fund to use for short-term, non-emergency spending. Above, lawmakers are shown at the state Capitol in June. (AP)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: October 2, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
State lawmakers — the same ones who have been approving spending plans for years that the Legislative Analyst’s Office says have billions of dollars in structural deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5091) despite the California Constitution’s requirement that budgets must be balanced — want you to believe they’re actually conscientious fiscal stewards.
That’s why in 2014, they won approval of a ballot measure that was sold to voters with the claim that it would force the Legislature to set aside 1.5% of general fund revenue to beef up the state’s Budget Stabilization Account — a “rainy day” fund that could be used to pay for specific state debts, starting with unfunded pension and retirement health care obligations.
It would also divert even more money to the fund when capital-gains revenue was surging, a common event in the Golden State due to all the wealthy individuals in Silicon Valley with stock options they can cash in when times are good.
But there was a mammoth loophole: Required contributions to the fund could be reduced or suspended after the governor and a majority of the Legislature declared a “budget emergency.”
That’s exactly what has happened over and over again. “Emergencies” were declared the last three completed fiscal years even though revenue was surging.
Now state lawmakers are back with another sham. Placed directly on the ballot by the Legislature, Proposition 2 would amend the Budget Stabilization Account by lifting the cap on how much could be contributed to it — something voters are being told would strengthen the account.
But that is built on the myth that lawmakers want to contribute more. The measure’s fine print (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/26/proposition-2-isnt-about-saving-money-its-another-sacramento-shell-game/) shows its real goal: to make it even easier for the state to avoid paying down long-term unfunded obligations by allowing lawmakers to use new rainy day funds to repay recent “budget borrowing.”
No on Proposition 2. It’s another fake reform meant to make Californians think state lawmakers are actually serious about their responsibilities.
The U-T also opposes Proposition 37 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_37,_Second_Mortgage_Homebuyer_Program_and_Revenue_Bond_Initiative_(2026)), which is less cynical than Proposition 2 but is equally unlikely to live up to the promises made about it.
The measure authorizes the state to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a middle-class down payment assistance program for purchasing newly constructed homes. Backers say it is structured in a way that ensures private bond investors, not state taxpayers, are on the hook for paying back the borrowing.
Its key provision: Eligible buyers would have to be able to make a 3% cash down payment on a home, but they could secure a fixed-rate second mortgage covering up to 17% of the purchase price. This in theory eliminates the traditional expectation of a 20% down payment.
What it doesn’t do in the slightest is to address the biggest reason California has a massive housing crisis: shelter’s extreme cost. Including condos, the median home price in the state is $775,000 (https://www.noradarealestate.com/blog/california-housing-market/). Median household income is about $99,000, according to a recent Census Bureau report (https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/CA/BZA210223). Whether a home purchase involves borrowing 80% or 97% of the sale price, the great majority of families are not going to be able to pay the resulting mortgage or mortgages.
Proposition 37 advocates somehow think that allowing qualified state residents to borrow more is a magic solution to the affordability crisis. But a Zillow calculator shows that with the interest rates available in recent months, a household income of at least $265,000 per year is generally necessary to buy a $775,000 home with a 3% down payment in California. Proposition 37 doesn’t change this daunting picture at all.
There are practical ways that the state could bring down the cost of housing. Leaders could ignore turf-protecting construction trade unions and incentivize use of the sturdy, durable prefabricated homes that now have big market shares in Japan and Great Britain. Advocates of Proposition 2 say they want to make it easier for state lawmakers to beef up the "rainy day" fund to help pay for long-term debt such as pension obligations. But the measure would actually make it easier to raid the fund to use for short-term, non-emergency spending. Above, lawmakers are shown at the state Capitol in June. (AP)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: October 2, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
State lawmakers — the same ones who have been approving spending plans for years that the Legislative Analyst’s Office says have billions of dollars in structural deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5091) despite the California Constitution’s requirement that budgets must be balanced — want you to believe they’re actually conscientious fiscal stewards.
That’s why in 2014, they won approval of a ballot measure that was sold to voters with the claim that it would force the Legislature to set aside 1.5% of general fund revenue to beef up the state’s Budget Stabilization Account — a “rainy day” fund that could be used to pay for specific state debts, starting with unfunded pension and retirement health care obligations.
It would also divert even more money to the fund when capital-gains revenue was surging, a common event in the Golden State due to all the wealthy individuals in Silicon Valley with stock options they can cash in when times are good.
But there was a mammoth loophole: Required contributions to the fund could be reduced or suspended after the governor and a majority of the Legislature declared a “budget emergency.”
That’s exactly what has happened over and over again. “Emergencies” were declared the last three completed fiscal years even though revenue was surging.
Now state lawmakers are back with another sham. Placed directly on the ballot by the Legislature, Proposition 2 would amend the Budget Stabilization Account by lifting the cap on how much could be contributed to it — something voters are being told would strengthen the account.
But that is built on the myth that lawmakers want to contribute more. The measure’s fine print (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/26/proposition-2-isnt-about-saving-money-its-another-sacramento-shell-game/) shows its real goal: to make it even easier for the state to avoid paying down long-term unfunded obligations by allowing lawmakers to use new rainy day funds to repay recent “budget borrowing.”
No on Proposition 2. It’s another fake reform meant to make Californians think state lawmakers are actually serious about their responsibilities.
The U-T also opposes Proposition 37 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_37,_Second_Mortgage_Homebuyer_Program_and_Revenue_Bond_Initiative_(2026)), which is less cynical than Proposition 2 but is equally unlikely to live up to the promises made about it.
The measure authorizes the state to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a middle-class down payment assistance program for purchasing newly constructed homes. Backers say it is structured in a way that ensures private bond investors, not state taxpayers, are on the hook for paying back the borrowing.
Its key provision: Eligible buyers would have to be able to make a 3% cash down payment on a home, but they could secure a fixed-rate second mortgage covering up to 17% of the purchase price. This in theory eliminates the traditional expectation of a 20% down payment.
What it doesn’t do in the slightest is to address the biggest reason California has a massive housing crisis: shelter’s extreme cost. Including condos, the median home price in the state is $775,000 (https://www.noradarealestate.com/blog/california-housing-market/). Median household income is about $99,000, according to a recent Census Bureau report (https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/CA/BZA210223). Whether a home purchase involves borrowing 80% or 97% of the sale price, the great majority of families are not going to be able to pay the resulting mortgage or mortgages.
Proposition 37 advocates somehow think that allowing qualified state residents to borrow more is a magic solution to the affordability crisis. But a Zillow calculator shows that with the interest rates available in recent months, a household income of at least $265,000 per year is generally necessary to buy a $775,000 home with a 3% down payment in California. Proposition 37 doesn’t change this daunting picture at all.
There are practical ways that the state could bring down the cost of housing. Leaders could ignore turf-protecting construction trade unions and incentivize use of the sturdy, durable prefabricated homes that now have big market shares in Japan and Great Britain. They could ignore revenue-protecting trial lawyers and fix flawed state rules that incentivize lawsuits against condo builders.

L E G I S L A T I V E A N A LY S T ’ S O F F I C E 1
Why Are California’s Revenues Volatile?
 Revenues Are Volatile. From year to year, revenues can grow very
quickly or contract quickly.
 Reasons for Volatility. The personal income tax (PIT) makes up
most of the General Fund revenues. Taxable personal income is more
volatile than the overall economy, primarily because: (1) incomes of
high-income taxpayers are more sensitive to changes in the economy
and asset markets and (2) the state’s progressive rate structure
concentrates taxes on these volatile incomes.
 Volatility Presents Two Related but Separate Issues. Reserves,
ideally separate ones, can address two distinct challenges:
(1) forecast error, and (2) downside risk.

Limitations of the Current Reserve Policy
 A reserve policy “performs well” if it meets the central goal of
reserves—that is, it allows the state to save enough so that the state
can pay for spending on its core services when revenues drop.
 Our analysis uses simulation-based tools—similar to those used
in insurance markets and the state’s pension system—that use
information about the past to forecast many different variations of
the future. These are reported across 50 years and thousands of
simulations.

State lawmakers — the same ones who have been approving spending plans for years that the Legislative Analyst’s Office says have billions of dollars in structural deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5091) despite the California Constitution’s requirement that budgets must be balanced — want you to believe they’re actually conscientious fiscal stewards.
That’s why in 2014, they won approval of a ballot measure that was sold to voters with the claim that it would force the Legislature to set aside 1.5% of general fund revenue to beef up the state’s Budget Stabilization Account — a “rainy day” fund that could be used to pay for specific state debts, starting with unfunded pension and retirement health care obligations.
It would also divert even more money to the fund when capital-gains revenue was surging, a common event in the Golden State due to all the wealthy individuals in Silicon Valley with stock options they can cash in when times are good.
But there was a mammoth loophole: Required contributions to the fund could be reduced or suspended after the governor and a majority of the Legislature declared a “budget emergency.”
That’s exactly what has happened over and over again. “Emergencies” were declared the last three completed fiscal years even though revenue was surging.
Now state lawmakers are back with another sham. Placed directly on the ballot by the Legislature, Proposition 2 would amend the Budget Stabilization Account by lifting the cap on how much could be contributed to it — something voters are being told would strengthen the account.

No on Proposition 2. It’s another fake reform meant to make Californians think state lawmakers are actually serious about their responsibilities.
The U-T also opposes Proposition 37 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_37,_Second_Mortgage_Homebuyer_Program_and_Revenue_Bond_Initiative_(2026)), which is less cynical than Proposition 2 but is equally unlikely to live up to the promises made about it.
The measure authorizes the state to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a middle-class down payment assistance program for purchasing newly constructed homes. Backers say it is structured in a way that ensures private bond investors, not state taxpayers, are on the hook for paying back the borrowing.
Its key provision: Eligible buyers would have to be able to make a 3% cash down payment on a home, but they could secure a fixed-rate second mortgage covering up to 17% of the purchase price. This in theory eliminates the traditional expectation of a 20% down payment.
What it doesn’t do in the slightest is to address the biggest reason California has a massive housing crisis: shelter’s extreme cost. Median household income is about $99,000, according to a recent Census Bureau report (https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/CA/BZA210223). Whether a home purchase involves borrowing 80% or 97% of the sale price, the great majority of families are not going to be able to pay the resulting mortgage or mortgages.
Proposition 37 advocates somehow think that allowing qualified state residents to borrow more is a magic solution to the affordability crisis. - **Broad, substantive coalition**: CA Professional Firefighters, LA Area Chamber of Commerce, CA Hospital Association, CA Primary Care Association, State Board of Education President Linda Darling-Hammond, League of Women Voters, SPUR, Xavier Becerra; SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy, Mercury News/East Bay Times, Daily Californian all endorse yes. - *"Cancels your tax rebate."* The Gann rebate has triggered **once in 45+ years** (1987); Prop 111 (1990) requires excess in **two consecutive years**, split half to schools. Withdrawal limits (max 50% in year one) and the definition of "budget emergency" are unchanged.
- *"Debt menu enables more borrowing."* Letting set-asides repay internal loans, Medi-Cal loans and settle-up does relieve General Fund pressure, and using it on the federal UI principal shifts a cost from employers to the state without fixing UI (a valid CalBudgetCenter critique). But these are **real liabilities** on a ~$29B "wall of debt," and the payment stream is constitutionally protected from suspension.
- *"Doesn't fix the structural deficit."* True — it manages volatility rather than its cause, and in some boom years it takes hundreds of millions to >$1B "off the table" from near-term needs (plus less infrastructure spillover). That's the intended trade-off.

**Bottom line:** the measure is directionally correct, endorsed by the state's own nonpartisan fiscal analyst as a first step toward what it recommends, costs taxpayers nothing new, and improves resilience against California's most severe and well-documented budget weakness. Its flaws are that it doesn't go far enough — which isn't a reason to reject it.

## Yes

**Vote YES on Proposition 2** (Nov 3, 2026 — "Increases State's Rainy Day Fund," ACA 20 / "Save for California's Future Act").

**Note:** the URL you gave now serves the **2026** ballot, not 2024. This Prop 2 is *not* the $10B school facilities bond from 2024 — it's a legislative constitutional amendment changing budget-reserve rules.

### What it actually does
1. **Doubles the BSA cap** from 10% → 20% of General Fund tax revenues.
2. **Captures more in boom years**: capital gains revenue above 10% of GF taxes is set aside at 150% (currently 100% above 8%).
3. **Extends mandatory extra debt payments** from 2030 → 2040, and broadens eligible debts (Prop 98 settle-up, internal "budgetary borrowing," Medi-Cal loans, the ~$20B federal UI loan). These payments still **cannot be suspended even in a budget emergency**.
4. **Fixes a backwards Gann-limit rule**: reserve deposits stop counting as "spending" when made; they count when *withdrawn*.

### Why yes
- **It follows the nonpartisan experts — and stops short of them.** The LAO's *Rethinking California's Reserve Policy* (Apr 2025) and its Feb 2026 Senate Budget presentation found current rules cover only **~30%** of funding shortfalls over 50 years; the Prop 2 package covers **~50%**. The LAO recommended going *further* (50% cap by 2055, covering ~75%), starting with "20 percent to take effect immediately after the next statewide election." It called the appropriations-limit change "**reasonable**." Prop 2 is a partial version of the analyst's own recommendation.
- **The problem is real and documented.** The top 1% pay ~50% of California's income tax; the state swung from a ~$100B surplus to cumulative budget problems of $82B in three years, and faces an **$18.5B structural operating deficit in 2026-27**. LAO notes recession revenue losses can exceed 50% of GF revenues.
- **Current law actively penalizes saving.** Deposits count against the spending cap while withdrawals don't — so saving in a boom year pushes the state over the Gann limit. Removing that perverse incentive is genuine reform. Even the **Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association concedes** the reserve/Gann changes "make sense from the perspective of addressing revenue volatility"; its NO is only because it wants *more* Gann restoration — i.e., "not enough," not "harmful."
- **No new taxes, no bonds, no cost to local government.** Pure budgeting rules. Passed the Assembly **59-8** and Senate **29-2**, with one Republican (Josh Hoover) voting yes.
- **Broad, substantive coalition**: CA Professional Firefighters, LA Area Chamber of Commerce, CA Hospital Association, CA Primary Care Association, State Board of Education President Linda Darling-Hammond, League of Women Voters, SPUR, Xavier Becerra; SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy, Mercury News/East Bay Times, Daily Californian all endorse yes. PPIC final poll: **61%–38%**.

### The real objections — and why they don't outweigh it
- *"Cancels your tax rebate."* The Gann rebate has triggered **once in 45+ years** (1987); Prop 111 (1990) requires excess in **two consecutive years**, split half to schools. The state currently has **$27.3B of room** under the limit, and Prop 2 doesn't exempt the money permanently — withdrawals count. This is largely theoretical.
- *"They'll just raid it."* Fair: the same Legislature suspended a **$5.4B** BSA true-up while placing this on the ballot, and the BSA sits at $15.1B (~6.7% of GF revenue, below even the current cap). Prop 2 also lets the May Revision serve as the emergency proclamation. But this means the cap raise is **not self-executing** — an argument that Prop 2 is *insufficient*, not that it's damaging. Withdrawal limits (max 50% in year one) and the definition of "budget emergency" are unchanged.
- *"Debt menu enables more borrowing."* Letting set-asides repay internal loans, Medi-Cal loans and settle-up does relieve General Fund pressure, and using it on the federal UI principal shifts a cost from employers to the state without fixing UI (a valid CalBudgetCenter critique). But these are **real liabilities** on a ~$29B "wall of debt," and the payment stream is constitutionally protected from suspension.
- *"Doesn't fix the structural deficit."* True — it manages volatility rather than its cause, and in some boom years it takes hundreds of millions to >$1B "off the table" from near-term needs (plus less infrastructure spillover). That's the intended trade-off.

**Bottom line:** the measure is directionally correct, endorsed by the state's own nonpartisan fiscal analyst as a first step toward what it recommends, costs taxpayers nothing new, and improves resilience against California's most severe and well-documented budget weakness. Its flaws are that it doesn't go far enough — which isn't a reason to reject it.

## Yes

**Vote YES on Proposition 2** (Nov 3, 2026 — "Increases State's Rainy Day Fund," ACA 20 / "Save for California's Future Act").

**Note:** the URL you gave now serves the **2026** ballot, not 2024. This Prop 2 is *not* the $10B school facilities bond from 2024 — it's a legislative constitutional amendment changing budget-reserve rules.

### What it actually does
1. **Doubles the BSA cap** from 10% → 20% of General Fund tax revenues.
2. **Captures more in boom years**: capital gains revenue above 10% of GF taxes is set aside at 150% (currently 100% above 8%).
3. **Extends mandatory extra debt payments** from 2030 → 2040, and broadens eligible debts (Prop 98 settle-up, internal "budgetary borrowing," Medi-Cal loans, the ~$20B federal UI loan). These payments still **cannot be suspended even in a budget emergency**.
4. **Fixes a backwards Gann-limit rule**: reserve deposits stop counting as "spending" when made; they count when *withdrawn*.

### Why yes
- **It follows the nonpartisan experts — and stops short of them.** The LAO's *Rethinking California's Reserve Policy* (Apr 2025) and its Feb 2026 Senate Budget presentation found current rules cover only **~30%** of funding shortfalls over 50 years; the Prop 2 package covers **~50%**. The LAO recommended going *further* (50% cap by 2055, covering ~75%), starting with "20 percent to take effect immediately after the next statewide election." It called the appropriations-limit change "**reasonable**." Prop 2 is a partial version of the analyst's own recommendation.
- **The problem is real and documented.** The top 1% pay ~50% of California's income tax; the state swung from a ~$100B surplus to cumulative budget problems of $82B in three years, and faces an **$18.5B structural operating deficit in 2026-27**. LAO notes recession revenue losses can exceed 50% of GF revenues.
- **Current law actively penalizes saving.** Deposits count against the spending cap while withdrawals don't — so saving in a boom year pushes the state over the Gann limit. Removing that perverse incentive is genuine reform. Even the **Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association concedes** the reserve/Gann changes "make sense from the perspective of addressing revenue volatility"; its NO is only because it wants *more* Gann restoration — i.e., "not enough," not "harmful."
- **No new taxes, no bonds, no cost to local government.** Pure budgeting rules. Passed the Assembly **59-8** and Senate **29-2**, with one Republican (Josh Hoover) voting yes.
- **Broad, substantive coalition**: CA Professional Firefighters, LA Area Chamber of Commerce, CA Hospital Association, CA Primary Care Association, State Board of Education President Linda Darling-Hammond, League of Women Voters, SPUR, Xavier Becerra; SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy, Mercury News/East Bay Times, Daily Californian all endorse yes. PPIC final poll: **61%–38%**.

### The real objections — and why they don't outweigh it
- *"Cancels your tax rebate."* The Gann rebate has triggered **once in 45+ years** (1987); Prop 111 (1990) requires excess in **two consecutive years**, split half to schools. The state currently has **$27.3B of room** under the limit, and Prop 2 doesn't exempt the money permanently — withdrawals count. This is largely theoretical.
- *"They'll just raid it."* Fair: the same Legislature suspended a **$5.4B** BSA true-up while placing this on the ballot, and the BSA sits at $15.1B (~6.7% of GF revenue, below even the current cap). Prop 2 also lets the May Revision serve as the emergency proclamation. But this means the cap raise is **not self-executing** — an argument that Prop 2 is *insufficient*, not that it's damaging. Withdrawal limits (max 50% in year one) and the definition of "budget emergency" are unchanged.
- *"Debt menu enables more borrowing."* Letting set-asides repay internal loans, Medi-Cal loans and settle-up does relieve General Fund pressure, and using it on the federal UI principal shifts a cost from employers to the state without fixing UI (a valid CalBudgetCenter critique). But these are **real liabilities** on a ~$29B "wall of debt," and the payment stream is constitutionally protected from suspension.
- *"Doesn't fix the structural deficit."* True — it manages volatility rather than its cause, and in some boom years it takes hundreds of millions to >$1B "off the table" from near-term needs (plus less infrastructure spillover). That's the intended trade-off.

**Bottom line:** the measure is directionally correct, endorsed by the state's own nonpartisan fiscal analyst as a first step toward what it recommends, costs taxpayers nothing new, and improves resilience against California's most severe and well-documented budget weakness. Its flaws are that it doesn't go far enough — which isn't a reason to reject it.

# Proposition 2
### ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
#### Background
Districts must get at least 55 percent of their voters to approve the sale of local bonds.
